You can ask Claude to review and remove rules it made for itself, and we're working on reducing overcaution in future models. We’re not in the practice of intentionally disrupting users’ work.

At the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal, reporters asked East German swimming coaches why their teenage female athletes suddenly had deep baritone voices and massive, heavily muscled shoulders.

The coaches laughed. They told the press they were in Montreal to swim, not to sing.

Newspapers printed the joke and moved on. When an American swimmer pointed out the obvious, that something in the pool wasn't right, sportswriters across the United States turned on her instead.

Her name was Shirley Babashoff.

She was nineteen years old, from Fountain Valley, California, and she had spent more than half her life preparing for that pool. Since the age of eight, she had trained under coach Mark Schubert at the Mission Viejo Nadadores club, waking up in the dark to swim ten thousand meters a day before and after high school.

At the 1972 Munich Games, she had won Olympic gold at fifteen. By 1976, holding multiple national records, she arrived in Montreal as the anchor of the American women's team.

Once the races began, the East German women dismantled every expectation in the aquatic center. They won eleven of the thirteen swimming gold medals and shattered world records in nearly every event.

Shirley swam the races of her life. She broke her own American records and walked away with four silver medals, posting times that would have guaranteed gold in almost any other era.

The American press expected her to smile on the podium and graciously congratulate the swimmers who beat her.

Shirley refused to play along. She stated plainly what everyone in the building could see: her competitors had developed deep voices and physiques unlike anything ever seen in women's swimming.

She wasn't media-trained, and she didn't hide her frustration when reporters pushed leading questions. She gave blunt answers and flatly refused to fake a smile for the cameras when she felt cheated on the world stage.

At the time, the International Olympic Committee had no reliable test to detect anabolic steroids, and Cold War politics prioritized keeping up the appearance of fair play. The United States Olympic Committee offered Shirley zero public defense.

American sportswriters found it far easier to attack an outspoken nineteen-year-old than to investigate an international sports machine. Columns across the country dubbed her "Surly Shirley," branding her a bitter runner-up and an embarrassment to American sportsmanship.

On the final day of the swimming events in Montreal, Shirley stepped onto the starting blocks for the 4×100-meter freestyle relay.

Her teammates, Kim Peyton, Wendy Boglioli, and Jill Sterkel, kept the race tight. When Shirley dove in for the anchor leg, she was swimming head-to-head against Kornelia Ender, the East German star who had already claimed four gold medals.

Shirley swam her leg in 55.48 seconds. The American women hit the wall in 3:44.82, beating East Germany by less than a second to win the gold medal.

It was the only women's swimming race the East Germans lost in the entire 1976 Olympics.

Even that victory couldn't shake the label the press had pinned on her. Shirley retired shortly after Montreal at nineteen years old, remembered by much of the public simply as the swimmer who complained.

Then, in 1989, the Berlin Wall fell.

In the early 1990s, the newly unified German government opened the archives of the Stasi, East Germany's secret police. Inside those files was a classified government directive called State Plan 14.25, a state-sponsored doping program engineered to prove communist superiority through Olympic medals.

The records laid out the exact milligrams of synthetic testosterone given to teenage girls. Doctors had handed thirteen- and fourteen-year-old swimmers little blue pills in locker rooms and at training tables, telling them they were vitamins. The pills were Oral-Turinabol, a potent anabolic steroid, administered in doses higher than those given to adult male weightlifters.

In the late 1990s, the doctors, coaches, and officials behind the program were put on trial in Berlin. Former East German athletes testified in court about failing livers, heart conditions, and severe birth defects in their children, victims of their own government.

Every allegation Shirley Babashoff had made in 1976 was proven as documented fact.

Still, the International Olympic Committee never changed the official record books, and the medals were never redistributed. Shirley went home to California, where she spent more than thirty years delivering mail for the United States Postal Service.
The 1976 times still stand.

She was asked to lose gracefully to a lie, and she chose to tell the truth even when her own country called her bitter for it. Why is it so often easier for people to punish the person pointing out an obvious unfairness than to confront the system behind it?

Release Notes: v1.0.92

Features:

• Positional prompts without `-p` now run headless and print their reply when the process has no terminal for the TUI
• MCP tool results that contain images now include those images in headless streaming and JSON output
• Clickable `file://` links to local files now open the file the same way bare paths do

• Question cards in minimal mode now keep the first option visible instead of scrolling it off-screen
• Headless runs (`grok -p`) now stop after 5 minutes of no model output instead of hanging indefinitely
• Session resume errors now give the same helpful instruction on every route instead of suggesting the TUI picker

Performance:

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

quote.name: Elena
quote.text:
one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.
-there’s a secondary problem though - even when we have beneficial tech, we may lack the will to diffuse it. waymo and GLP-1s, for example, can save lives (neurosurgeons have compared waymo’s safety results to a treatment so effective that continuing to give patients a placebo would become unethical). and yet evidence of a benefit doesn’t automatically produce the will to act on it.
-the reality described in deep utopia ameliorates this by imagining that our psychology might one day become changeable too. i might want an environment that suits my temperament but i can also go the opposite direction and manipulate myself to become more adventurous or less anxious, in other words, more suited to my environment. the interesting possibility is having more agency over both worlds, external and internal. glps’ effect on appetite already suggests how technology can change the effort involved in pursuing a goal (though again, it is telling that not everyone who *should* be on peptides *are* despite the health benefits). the sci-fi version extends that possibility enormously.
-timing matters. bostrom reminds us that people continue to die while potentially lifesaving advances remain unavailable (he literally says “if nobody builds it, everyone dies” as a hypothetical inversion of yudkowsky/soares’ book).

i’d like ai to make it easier for people to live very different lives, without creating this burden of proof that theirs is the best one.

• Commit to providing service for 10 years.
• Continue to comply with federal performance testing requirements.

The agreement will save American taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars while accelerating high-speed internet access in underserved rural communities.

In exchange, SpaceX would be exempt from most BEAD-related financial audits, procurement requirements and administrative reporting, while remaining subject to network performance testing.

An internal Claude model just found a proof of the algebraic analogue of P vs NP, known as Valiant’s conjecture

Claude is credited as the author of the 70-page paper and the Lean proof passed automated checks.

If you remember the determinant of a 2×2 matrix, it’s ad − bc. Change it to ad + bc and you get the “permanent.” The same idea works for larger matrices. Both expressions grow to billions of terms by the time you reach a 13×13 matrix, yet the determinant has a shortcut that lets you skip writing them all out.›

Could there be a shortcut like that for the permanent? The paper claims that over the real numbers, even the best possible sequence of additions and multiplications eventually takes more steps than any fixed polynomial in the matrix size.

Read here: https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2611.vp-vnp-arithmetic-lower-bounds

ref.name: Maye Musk
ref.text: The first room at the front door was Elon‘s. There was a mattress on the floor. When the young people arrived and were dancing upstairs, I thought the floor was going to collapse so I moved the mattress to the wall. I assumed just the middle would collapse. I put the door money in a shoebox. When I saw it was quite a lot, I fetched a kitchen knife in case someone tried to take it away from me. I was also the coat check girl. When the police arrived after midnight due to complaints about the noise, I answered the door in my pajamas. That night I slept on the mattress on the floor. It was still better than sleeping on the ground in the Kalahari desert with hyenas, lions, snakes or scorpions visiting us. Memories from my childhood made me appreciate a mattress.

quote.name: Eva Fo𝕏 🦊 Claudius Nero's Legion
quote.text:
When Elon Musk was a student at the University of Pennsylvania, he was paying his own way through college. He and his roommate rented a cheap ten-bedroom house that had once been a frat house and began hosting weekend parties there, charging five dollars at the door. Elon later said he could make an entire month's rent in one night, and that somebody had to stay sober to run the party, so he did.

When Maye came to visit one weekend, she was quite surprised by it all, and then she did what Maye always does: she helped. She worked coat check and even guarded the cash, as he later joked, with a kitchen knife 😅

BREAKING: Aer Lingus Chief Customer Officer Susanne Carberry praises @Starlink as the airline expands free Starlink Wi-Fi to European flights following a “fantastic” customer response on North American routes.

“The response from our customers to Starlink Wi-Fi travelling to our North American destinations has been fantastic, so we’re delighted to start bringing that same experience to customers flying with us across Europe.

“Our customers expect to be able to stay connected wherever they are, and that doesn’t stop when they step onboard an aircraft.

“Bringing Starlink to our European fleet is about responding to that demand and giving customers the fast, reliable connectivity they increasingly expect when they travel.

“Whether it’s keeping the kids entertained, catching up on work or getting a head start on the holiday, we want our customers to have more choice in how they spend their time with us.”

— Susanne Carberry, Chief Customer Officer at Aer Lingus
